blurb: The model, where humans fit in it, and the risks it balances.

chapters.title: From Dark Factory to Software Garden
chapters.summary: Why we stopped calling it a dark factory. The metaphor that set the ambition, why it leaves people in the dark, and the garden that fits better: agents grow the code, humans tend the structure as growth wears it down.
chapters.tagline: Why we stopped calling it a dark factory.

chapters.title: The role of humans in the agentic SDLC
chapters.summary: Humans move to the edges: vision and validation, with agents implementing in the middle. And the answer to “how will I know the code is any good?”
chapters.tagline: Vision, validation and structure.

chapters.title: The organisation of agents
chapters.summary: Zoom from a colony of agents, through the processes they follow, into a codebase garden. Watch it run wild, then partly structured, then refactored into a structure that holds up at agentic speed.
chapters.tagline: The garden in 3D: jungle, partial structure, and structure under growth.

chapters.title: Two ways to lose
chapters.summary: Too careful loses the market; too careless loses trust. Engineering manages two trade-offs: speed against risk, and speed against complexity.
chapters.tagline: Weeds and drought: too careless, or too careful. It's the engineering part.

blurb: How you know it's any good, at agentic speed.

chapters.title: Agentic Loop Engineering
chapters.summary: TDD is the template: a hard correctness condition lets an agent climb to correctness. Then loops inside loops, escaped defects, trade-offs, and why it's engineering all the way down.
chapters.tagline: Irrigation: loops that climb to correctness.

chapters.title: There are no flaky tests
chapters.summary: An intermittent failure is a real defect, in the test or in the product. Why noisy signals break agent loops, how to control time, and why every fix should cover the whole class of defect.
chapters.tagline: Clean signals for the loops.

chapters.title: All software fails somewhere
chapters.summary: All software fails somewhere. Keep the signal non-negotiable, reason at compiler speed instead of human speed, stack integration and scenario tests to find the failure conditions, and feed them back so the defect rate falls as throughput rises.
chapters.tagline: Every garden has pests: find them early, and learn from each one.

chapters.title: Point them at a number
chapters.description: Telemetry is a test: agents in a write-build-deploy-load-measure loop hunt their own bottlenecks. Real examples from the Nano BPM engine and the Camunda SDKs, and what changes when agents start the work.
chapters.summary: Telemetry is a test. Agents in a change, build, deploy, load and measure loop hunt their own bottlenecks and disprove their own theories. Check the instruments, then give agents an objective and guardrails and let them find the work.
chapters.tagline: Rain gauges: measure the garden, and let the growers chase the number.

chapters.title: Zero-eyes PR approval
chapters.summary: Agents review and fix each other's pull requests until the review is clean. Humans stop reading every PR and start engineering the loop: what escapes it, and how to make it stronger.
chapters.tagline: Engineering the review loop instead of reading every PR.

blurb: Know where the model is reliable, and harden the edges at compiler speed.

chapters.title: Every model has an envelope
chapters.summary: Models aren't good or bad, or interchangeable. Map where yours is reliable, and harden the edges with structure.
chapters.tagline: Know where it's reliable; put the trellises where it's thin.

chapters.title: Rules that enforce themselves
chapters.summary: A rule in a document is advice; a rule in the build is a fact. The enforcement ladder, ratchets, narrow exceptions, an always-green baseline, and turning review comments into checks.
chapters.tagline: Trellises that agents can't lean past.

chapters.title: Derivation over duplication
chapters.summary: Write each fact once and generate the rest: seven SDKs from one spec, docs and help from compiled sources, a generator you fix instead of its output, and CI that proves nothing drifted.
chapters.tagline: One fact, one place: no twin plants to drift apart.

blurb: The tools agents use, and the gates they pass through.

chapters.title: Designing for agent users
chapters.summary: Agents use our tools too. Data rather than prose, one job per output channel, respecting the context budget, dry runs, self-describing help, and SDKs whose types and errors tell the truth. And one level down: a codebase designed for the agents that change it.
chapters.tagline: Tools shaped for the ones doing the growing.

chapters.title: Get to the eleventh
chapters.summary: Nobody one-shots good software. Guardrails make correctness cheap; fitness takes rounds. Prove an API before publishing with a network of consumers, user testing at scale by proxy, and grow that network as fast as the code.
chapters.tagline: Grown, not cast.

chapters.title: The merge button is part of the system
chapters.summary: Auto-merge is only as safe as what the branch refuses. Required checks that can actually fail, stable branches, settings drift across a fleet, a vulnerability-to-release loop with no human in it, and handing admin changes to humans.
chapters.tagline: The garden gate.

blurb: Rolling it out: people, teams, tools and bottlenecks.

chapters.title: The bottleneck moved
chapters.summary: The Theory of Constraints for agentic engineering: find where work waits, fix it, find the next one.
chapters.tagline: Find the constraint, fix it, repeat.

chapters.title: The constraint is mindset, not the model
chapters.summary: Same model, opposite results. The beliefs, incentives and learning curve that decide which.
chapters.tagline: Beliefs, incentives, the learning curve.

chapters.title: You are the skill
chapters.summary: Tools churn. Your judgement, encoded as skills, rules and checks, is what scales.
chapters.tagline: Encode your judgement so it scales.

chapters.title: Conway's Law still holds
chapters.summary: Features cross teams. Every repository declares what it owns, and a planning skill places each capability with its owner.
chapters.tagline: Plan with the owner, not around them.

chapters.title: Start with one garden
chapters.summary: Choose one codebase, prepare it, prove it, and let it seed the next.
chapters.tagline: Prepare, prove, then spread.

blurb: What happened when we did it: the numbers, from the git history.

chapters.title: Case study: the Cambrian explosion
chapters.description: One engineer, one SDK, measured from the git history: a hardened spec, seven language SDKs derived from it, generated tests, profiled workloads, and an approach that spread from one owner to a pod of three.
chapters.summary: One engineer went agentic. One SDK became 22 repositories and seven languages, and one owner became a pod of three.
chapters.tagline: A real garden: what grew, from the git history.

chapters.title: Case study: three shapes
chapters.description: Two more Camunda engineers who went agentic on their own: a product built in five weeks inside a fence, and a shared repository where each change waited longer but four times as many merged. Then all three compared: who decides a change is done?
chapters.summary: Three engineers, independently. A fence, a gate and a loop: where the speed went, and who decides a change is done.
chapters.tagline: Same agents, different settings, different shapes.

chapters.title: Case study: c8ctl, a shared garden
chapters.description: The Camunda 8 CLI, from a one-day one-shot to a structure 26 people build in. Each phase maps to a chapter: humans at the edges, agents as users, derivation and self-enforcing rules, no flaky tests, and a merge gate only green changes pass.
chapters.summary: Where the method left the SDKs: a one-shot CLI, hardened so incomplete commands are impossible, now grown by 26 people.
chapters.tagline: Many gardeners, one structure.

chapters.title: Conclusion: Agency, not AGENTS.md
chapters.description: Everyone has the same tools. The difference is the operator: curiosity, openness and a systems engineering mindset. Attitude comes before experience, and done right the outcome is more velocity, more innovation and, almost paradoxically, more stability.
chapters.summary: Same tools, different operators. Curiosity, openness and systems thinking bring velocity, innovation and, paradoxically, stability.
chapters.tagline: The gardener matters more than the tools.
